DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 24SMCV03583    Hearing Date: September 15, 2026    Dept: 205

Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District 

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

JOEL PEREZ,   

  

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

HCP 8631 HAYDEN LLC, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 24SMCV03583 

  

  Date: September 15, 2026 

  

  ORDER RE: 

  DEFENDANT POSSIBLE PRODUCTION,  

  INC.’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE  

  CROSS-COMPLAINT  

   

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a negligence and premises liability case.  Plaintiff fell from a chair at a property owned or managed by Defendant HCP 8631 Hayden LLC.  Plaintiff claims that HCP “negligently, carelessly, recklessly and/or wantonly managed, owned, maintained, operated, controlled, designed and/or safeguarded the premises ... such that a chair was allowed to fall into a state of disrepair and therefore prone to collapsing, thereby constituting a dangerous condition.”   

After filing his original complaint, Plaintiff filed two amendments substituting Defendant Possible Production, Inc. (“Possible”) for Doe 1, and Defendant Quality Control & Services (“Quality”) for Doe 2.  Possible filed an answer on March 2, 2025 which did not contain cross-claims.   

This hearing is on Possible’s motion for leave to file a cross-complaint against Quality (who on September 3, 2026 was named as a defendant in Plaintiff’s complaint).  Possible proposes to sue Quality for equitable indemnity, implied indemnity, apportionment of fault, contribution and declaratory relief.  Possible argues that Quality was responsible for the “ownership, maintenance, and/or control of the subject chair [which] was the intervening cause of Plaintiff’s alleged injuries.”  Possible claims that it did not file the cross-complaint earlier due to oversight.  It discovered that a third party owned or maintained the chair after the deposition of Carmen Bonilla in November 2025, and in the ensuing six months, Defendant diligently conducted an investigation in order to determine the identity of the third party.  There was no opposition filed as of the posting of this tentative ruling. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

Code of Civil Procedure section 428.10, subdivision (b), authorizes a party against whom a cause of action has been asserted to file a cross-complaint alleging a cause of action against a person alleged to be liable thereon, whether or not that person is already a party, when the proposed cause of action “(1) arises out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences as the cause brought against him or (2) asserts a claim, right, or interest in the property or controversy which is the subject of the cause brought against him.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.10, subd. (b).)  

A party may file a cross-complaint against a co-party or another person before the court sets a trial date. (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50(b).)  Here, trial has already been set (for March 22, 2027.)  Once a trial date has been set, the party must obtain leave of court, which “may be granted in the interest of justice at any time during the course of the action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50(c).)   

“Permission to file a permissive cross-complaint is solely within the trial court's discretion.” (Crocker Nat. Bank v. Emerald (1990) 221 Cal.App.3d 852, 864.) Factors considered are judicial efficiency, fairness to the parties, the interests of justice, and delay in seeking court's permission to file the cross-complaint. (Id.)   

DISCUSSION 

Possible’s proposed cross-claims against Quality are permissive.  While they arise from the same transaction and occurrence as Plaintiff’s complaint against Possible, indemnity and contribution claims generally do not accrue until a judgment or settlement is paid.  (Time for Living, Inc. v. Guy Hatfield Homes/All American Development Co., 230 Cal. App. 3d at 36.)  So Possible does not forfeit the claims by failing to bring them here, and accordingly, they are not compulsory cross-claims.  (Silver Organizations Ltd., 217 Cal. App. 3d at 98-99 

(policy behind compulsory claim statute (section 426.50 is to avoid forfeiture of claims).)  

For permissive cross-claims, the proper standard is whether the filing of the cross-claims serves the interest of justice.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50(c).)   The Court concludes it does so here.   

Plaintiff is suing Possible and Quality for injuries resulting from a defective chair that Plaintiff claims was negligently maintained.  Possible seeks to sue Quality whose alleged negligence Possible claims is an intervening cause of the accident.  Trying the actions together will avoid possible duplication of effort and inconsistencies and promote judicial efficiency.   

There is no evidence of delay on the part of Possible in seeking leave.  Possible represents that it was not aware of its potential claims against Quality until the deposition of a witness in November 2025, which prompted a six month investigation by Possible to identify Quality.   

Even if there is delay, Plaintiff has not argued it will be prejudiced by the amendment.  Indeed, Plaintiff has recently added Quality as a defendant.  Also, Plaintiff has not opposed Possible’s motion, thereby conceding the merits of the motion.  (See D.I. Chadbourne, Inc. v. Super. Ct. (1964) 60 Cal.2d 723, 728, fn. 4 [where nonmoving party fails to oppose a ground for a motion “it is assumed that [nonmoving party] concedes” that ground].) 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

   For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS the motion for leave to file cross-complaint.   

 
IT IS SO ORDERED. 

 

DATED:  September 16, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

Case Number: 25SMCV01600    Hearing Date: September 15, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

RALPH VALERA, JR., 

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

CITY OF WEST HOLLYWOOD, et al, 

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 25SMCV01600 

  Hearing Date: September 15, 2026 

  order RE: 

  CROSS-DEFENDANT MICHAEL  

  NICHOLAS JACKSON’S motion to  

  quash DEPOSITION SUBPOENAS  

  issued by defendant/CROSS- 

  COMPLAINANT CITY OF WEST  

  HOLLYWOOD  

  

 

 

 

 

 

This hearing is on Cross-Defendant Michael Nicholas Jackson’s motion to quash deposition subpoenas issued by Defendant/Cross-Complainant City of West Hollywood to Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, Esurance Property and Casualty Insurance Company, Progressive Casualty Insurance Company, and the DMV.   

Jackson argues that the subpoenas are overly broad as to time and scope, invade his right to privacy under the U.S. and California Constitution, and seek information that is irrelevant and not reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of relevant admissible evidence. 

This Department’s rules require that on a discovery motion, the parties must meet and confer to informally resolve their dispute, and when that fails, the parties must attend an informal discovery conference (IDC).  There is no record of an IDC on the issues raised in Jackson’s motion to quash.  Accordingly, the Court denies the motion to quash without prejudice.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.

Case Number: 25SMCV06313    Hearing Date: September 15, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

ROBERT H. AMES,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

CHRISTOPHER D. WALTON,  

 

Defendant. 

 

  Case No.:  25SMCV06313 

  

  Hearing Date: September 15, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  defendant christopher  

 walton’s special motion to  

 strike portions of plaintiff’s  

 complaint under the anti-slapp  

 statute  

 

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

 

This is a malicious prosecution case.  Plaintiff Robert Ames alleges that on September 12, 2022 Defendant Christopher Walton “created and disseminated a completely false 2-page written correspondence he labeled in bold capital letters “URGENT COMMUNIUCATION?” addressed it to the City of Santa Monica, the Police Chief, the City Attorney and the Mayor.”   

The letter purportedly contained “horrific vile descriptions of Plaintiff” and alleged Plaintiff had engaged in “false dangerous actions and crimes” upon Walton’s friend and sexual partner, Monique Eagle, as well as her minor children.  The letter also allegedly demanded a “No Knock Arrest Warrant” against Plaintiff, claiming “This is a dangerous life threatening situation that requires immediate action”  

As a result of Walton’s letter, Plaintiff claims the City Attorney for Santa Monica filed two “false” misdemeanor counts against Plaintiff in September 2023.  Plaintiff alleges that the charges were subsequently withdrawn by the state.   

In addition, Plaintiff also claims that Walton initiated a civil proceeding in the Los Angeles Superior Court, seeking a TRO against Plaintiff.  Plaintiff claims that Walton never served any of the court documents on her, which allowed Walton to “secure a 2-year permanent court order issued by the court against plaintiff under false light.”  Plaintiff is now suing Walton for malicious prosecution and intentional infliction of emotional distress.  Both parties are appearing in pro per. 

This hearing is on Walton’s special motion to strike.  Walton argues that Plaintiff’s entire complaint is based on his reporting to government agencies which constitutes protected activity.  Walton further argues that Plaintiff has no chance of prevailing on his claims because Plaintiff cannot meet the elements of a malicious prosecution claim as Walton did not bring any legal action against Plaintiff.  Additionally, Walton argues that the claims are time-barred as well as barred by the litigation privilege.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

“Litigation of an anti-SLAPP motion involves a two-step process. First, the moving defendant bears the burden of establishing that the challenged allegations or claims arise from protected activity in which the defendant has engaged.  Second, for each claim that does arise from protected activity, the plaintiff must show the claim has “at least ‘minimal merit.’  If the plaintiff cannot make this showing, the court will strike the claim.”  (Bonni v. St. Joseph Health System (2021) 11 Cal.5th 995, 1009.)   

DISCUSSION  

First Prong 

On the first prong, “courts are to consider the elements of the challenged claim and what actions by the defendant supply those elements and consequently form the basis for liability.  The defendant’s burden is to identify what acts each challenged claim rests on and to show how those acts are protected under a statutorily defined category of protected activity.”  (Bonni, 11 Cal.5th at 1009.)  “A defendant need only make a prima facie showing at this stage.”  (Ojjeh v. Brown (2019) 43 Cal.App.5th 1027, 1035–1036.)   

Here, Plaintiff alleges claims based on Walton’s allegedly false reporting to several government agencies, including the police, as well as his filing of a civil suit seeking a TRO.  Under California law, statements to the police are considered¿protected activity.¿(Comstock v. Aber¿(2012) 212 Cal.App.4th 931, 941.) This is because such communications arise from a person’s right to petition the¿government.¿  

Moreover, even allegedly false reports to the police constitute protected activity.  (Chabak v. Monroy¿(2007) 154 Cal.App.4th 1502, 1512¿[the defendant’s allegedly¿false report¿to police that the plaintiff inappropriately touched her was deemed¿protected activity¿because there was no uncontroverted evidence showing the¿report¿to be¿false];¿see also Siam v. Kizilbash¿(2005) 130 Cal.App.4th 1563, 1569–1570¿ [defendant’s allegedly¿false report¿to school official was¿protected activity, notwithstanding plaintiff's allegation of falsity, because no uncontroverted evidence showed that it was¿false].)  The mere allegation that the defendant engaged in unlawful activities is not sufficient to render the defendant’s alleged actions unlawful as a matter of law and outside the protection of the Anti-SLAPP statute.  (See¿Dwight R. v. Christy B.¿(2013) 212 Cal.App.4th 697, 712.) 

Of course, where a defendant admits that his report to the police (or any other governmental agency) was false, the report no longer constitutes protected activity.  (Lefebvre v. Lefebvre¿(2011) 199 Cal.App.4th 696.)  In Lefebvre, a wife falsely reported to police that her husband had threatened to kill her and her children.¿(Id.¿at 700.)¿In response, the husband filed an action against the wife and her co-conspirator for, inter alia, malicious prosecution, false arrest, and intentional infliction of emotional distress.¿(Id.¿at 701.)¿In affirming the trial court’s order denying the wife's special motion to strike, the court in¿Lefebvre¿held that because the wife’s report to the police was¿admittedly false¿and therefore illegal, it did not constitute conduct in furtherance of her constitutional rights of petition or free speech. (Id.¿at¿967.)  In this case, however, Walton makes no admission that his reporting was false.   

In addition, Walton’s filing of the lawsuit against Plaintiff (to secure a restraining order) clearly constitutes protected activity.  ¿“The filing¿of lawsuits is an aspect of the¿First Amendment¿right of petition” (Soukup v. Law Offices of Herbert Hafif¿(2006) 39 Cal.4th 260, 291), and thus is a protected activity under the anti-¿SLAPP statute.¿(Nunez v. Pennisi¿(2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 861, 872 [malicious prosecution];¿Wallace, 196 Cal.App.4th at 1182–1193 [unlawful detainer].)¿ 

Second Prong 

Once a defendant demonstrates that protected conduct is at issue, the plaintiff must show that the complaint is both legally sufficient and supported by a sufficient prima facie showing of facts to sustain a favorable judgment if the evidence submitted by the plaintiff is credited.  (See Navellier v. Sletten (2002) 29 Cal.4th 82, 88-89.)  “Precisely because the statute (1) permits early intervention in lawsuits alleging unmeritorious causes of action that implicate free speech concerns, and (2) limits opportunity to conduct discovery, the plaintiff’s burden of establishing a probability of prevailing is not high: We do not weigh credibility, nor do we evaluate the weight of the evidence.  Instead, we accept as true all evidence favorable to the plaintiff and assess the defendant’s evidence only to determine if it defeats the plaintiff’s submission as a matter of law. Only a cause of action that lacks ‘even minimal merit’ constitutes SLAPP.”  (Overstock.com, Inc. v. Gradient Analytics, Inc. (2007) 151 Cal.App.4th 688, 699.)  

The SLAPP statute’s second element--a “probability of prevailing”--means a “reasonable probability of prevailing, not prevailing by a preponderance of the evidence.  For this reason, a court must apply a ‘summary-judgment-like’ test, accepting as true the evidence favorable to the plaintiff and evaluating the defendant’s evidence only to determine whether the defendant has defeated the plaintiff’s evidence as a matter of law.”  (Gerbosi v. Gaims, Weil, West & Epstein, LLP (2011) 193 Cal.App.4th 435, 444.) 

 

Walton argues that because the prosecutor initiated the proceeding, he cannot be sued for malicious prosecution and therefore, Plaintiff has no probability of prevailing.  But that is not the law.   

A private person may be civilly liable for malicious prosecution of a criminal action without personally signing the complaint that initiated the action. (Zucchet, 229 Cal.App.4th at 1481.)¿The test is whether the defendant was “instrumental in causing the prosecution.” (Sullivan, 12 Cal.3d at 720.)  The defendant may be liable for initiating, instigating, procuring, or being actively instrumental in putting in motion the criminal action.¿(Leon, supra, 14 Cal.5th at 921;¿Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. Bear Stearns & Co.¿(1990) 50 Cal.3d 1118, 1131, fn. 11.)  A defendant who seeks out the police or prosecutorial authorities and falsely reports facts to them indicating the plaintiff committed a crime can be liable for malicious prosecution.¿(Sullivan, 12 Cal.3d at 720.)  

However, the Court agrees that Plaintiff has not sufficiently shown that the criminal proceedings were terminated in her favor.  Plaintiff only alleges that the charges were dismissed.  “It is not enough, however, merely to show that the proceeding¿was dismissed.” (Jaffe v. Stone¿(1941) 18 Cal.2d 146, 150.)¿If a dismissal “is of such a nature as to indicate the¿innocence of the accused, it is a favorable termination sufficient to satisfy the requirement. If, however, the dismissal is on technical grounds, for procedural reasons, or for any other reason not inconsistent with [his] guilt, it does not constitute a favorable termination.” (Id.) Thus, “[w]hen the proceeding terminates other than on the merits, the court must¿examine the reasons for termination¿to see if the disposition reflects the opinion of the court or the prosecuting party that the action would not succeed.” (Susag v. City of Lake Forest¿(2002) 94 Cal.App.4th 1401, 1411, italics added.)¿ Ames cites no evidence indicating the reason(s) for the dismissal, and thus he cannot establish favorable termination as a matter of law. (Doe v. San Diego-Imperial Council¿(2017) 16 Cal.App.5th 301, 315.)¿ 

As to the civil proceedings initiated by Walton, the complaint does not allege at all that they were terminated in Plaintiff’s favor.  To the contrary, the Complaint alleges that Walton was able to secure a two-year permanent restraining order against him.  Accordingly, as to this civil proceeding as well, Plaintiff cannot state a malicious prosecution claim.   

As to the intentional infliction of emotional distress claim, the Court concludes it is barred by the litigation privilege.  Section 47, subdivision (b), “establishes a privilege that bars liability in tort for the making of certain statements.” (Hagberg v. California Federal Bank (2004) 32 Cal.4th 350, 360.)  Subdivision (b)(3) and (b)(4) confer immunity from civil liability for statements made in any “official proceeding authorized by law” and “the initiation or course of any other proceeding authorized by law…”.  It is an “absolute privilege” and bars all tort causes of action except a claim for malicious prosecution.  (Whelan v. Wolford (1958) 164 Cal.App.2d 689, 694.)  

“[I]t is now well established that the litigation privilege applies without regard to ‘motives, morals, ethics or intent.’ (Silberg, 50 Cal.3d at . 220.) The litigation privilege is simply a test of connectedness or logical relationship to litigation. (Blanchard v. DIRECTV, Inc., 123 Cal.App.4th at 922.)  

The litigation privilege “serves broad goals of guaranteeing access to the judicial process, promoting the zealous representation by counsel of their clients, and reinforcing the traditional function of the trial as the engine for the determination of truth. Applying the litigation privilege to some forms of unlawful litigation-related activity may advance those broad goals notwithstanding the occasional unfair result in an individual case.” (Flatley v. Mauro (2006) 39 Cal.4th 299, 324.)  “To achieve this purpose of curtailing derivative lawsuits, the courts have interpreted the litigation privilege broadly.” (Feldman v. 1100 Park Lane Associates (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 1467, 1485.)  Any doubt about whether the privilege applies is resolved in favor of applying it. (Optional Capital, Inc. v. Akin Gump, Strauss, Hauer & Feld LLP (2017) 18 Cal.App.5th 95, 116.)   

Here, the litigation privilege bars Plaintiff’s IIED claim which is based solely on Walton’s allegedly false reporting to government agencies and his initiation of a civil proceeding to obtain a TRO against Plaintiff.  Accordingly, the Court concludes that Plaintiff has no probability of prevailing on either claim, and the Court grants the special motion to strike without leave to amend. 

CONCLUSION 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS the special motion to strike without leave to amend.   

DATED: September 15, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

Case Number: 25SMCV06530    Hearing Date: September 15, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

HNM PROPERTY MANAGEMENT, INC.,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

MICHAEL ANTHONY CLINTON, et al.,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 25SMCV06530 

  Hearing Date: September 15, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  PLAINTIFF’S motion for  

  terminating sanctions OR IN THE  

  ALTERNATIVE for issue and  

  evidentiary sanctions and for  

  monetary sanctions 

 

 

  

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a fraud case.  Plaintiff HNM Property Management, Inc. alleges that Defendant Michael Anthony Clinton solicited funds from its CEO for various deals involving real property located in California, Mississippi and Alabama.  One of the properties was bought through Clinton’s company, Defendant Micro-Boutique Venice LLC.  The various debts were later assigned to HNM.  A portion of the debts was guaranteed by Defendant Tiffany Clinton. 

Plaintiff claims that Clinton never intended, and had no ability to repay, the funds.  Further, as to one of the properties, the mortgagee initiated foreclosure proceedings, and Clinton represented to HNM that he would retain counsel to protect HNM’s interest, but he failed to do so.   

Plaintiff served four sets of discovery on Defendants: special interrogatories (“SROGs”), form interrogatories (“FROGs”), requests for production (“RFPs”), and requests for admissions (“RFAs”).  Defendants failed to serve initial verified responses by the statutory deadline, and Plaintiff filed three motions to compel and one motion to deem the RFAs admitted.  Defendants did not oppose any of the motions.  The Court granted all four motions on July 1, 2026, and sanctioned Defendants and their counsel jointly and severally, in the amount of $5,367.00. 

This hearing is on Plaintiff’s motion for terminating sanctions.  Plaintiff represents that Defendants have still not served their responses to the discovery requests, and they have also failed to pay the sanctions ordered by the Court.  Plaintiff argues that terminating sanctions are warranted because less severe sanctions have not induced Defendants to comply with their discovery obligations.  Plaintiff also seeks sanctions in the amount of $13,900 plus $83 in costs. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

 

California Code of Civil Procedure section 2023.030 permits courts to impose sanctions against anyone engaging in conduct that constitutes a misuse of the discovery process. Section 2023.010 provides a non-exhaustive list of conduct that is considered misuse of the discovery process, including failing to respond or to submit to an authorized method of discovery, providing evasive answers, and asserting unmeritorious objections. (Cal. Civ. Proc. § 2023.010(d), (g).)  

Further, Code of Civil Procedure section 2023.030 subdivision (d) gives courts the authority to issue a terminating sanction by one of four following orders: (1) an order striking out the pleadings or parts of the pleadings of any party engaging in misuse of the discovery process; (2) an order staying further proceedings until an order for discovery is obeyed; (3) an order dismissing the action, or any part of the action, of that party; or (4) an order rendering a default judgment against that party.  

In determining whether to impose terminating sanctions, trial courts must consider the totality of the circumstances, including whether the actions were willful; the detriment to the propounding party; and the number of informal and formal attempts to obtain the discovery. (Lang v. Hochman (2000) 77 Cal.App,4th 1225, 1246.) 

The trial court has broad discretion in selecting discovery sanctions, subject to reversal only for abuse. (Reedy v. Bussell (2007) 148 Cal.App.4th 1272, 1293; Miranda v. 21st Century Ins. Co. (2004) 117 Cal.App.4th 913, 928–929.)  The trial court should consider both the conduct being sanctioned and its effect on the party seeking discovery and, in choosing a sanction, should “attempt[] to tailor the sanction to the harm caused by the withheld discovery.” (Do It Urself Moving & Storage, Inc. v. Brown, Leifer, Slatkin & Berns (1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 27, 36.) 

The discovery statutes evince an incremental approach to discovery sanctions, starting with monetary sanctions and ending with the ultimate sanction of termination.  “Discovery sanctions should be appropriate to the dereliction, and should not exceed that which is required to protect the interests of the party entitled to but denied discovery.” (Laguna Auto Body v. Farmers Ins. Exchange, 231 Cal.App.3d at p. 487.)  If a lesser sanction fails to curb misuse, a greater sanction is warranted; continuing misuses of the discovery process warrant incrementally harsher sanctions until the sanction is reached that will curb the abuse.  (Doppes v. Bentley Motors, Inc. (2009) 174 Cal. App. 4th 967, 992.)     

DISCUSSION 

As a threshold matter, the Court considers the timeliness of Defendant’s opposition.  The deadline to file an opposition is 9 court days from the hearing date or September 4, 2026.  (Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1005(b) and Cal. Rules of Court, Rule 3.1300.)  Defendant filed its opposition on September 11, 2026.  Counsel does not provide any explanation for filing the Opposition late.  While counsel has a pending motion to withdraw, it did not impede Counsel from filing the untimely opposition so it should not have prevented counsel from filing a timely opposition.  The Court declines to consider the late opposition. 

The Court now turns to the merits of the motion.  Because terminating sanctions are the most “drastic” penalty, they are typically a “last resort” to be “used sparingly”.  (Siry Investment, L.P. v. Farkhondehpour (2020) 45 Cal.App.5th 1098, 1118.)  However, they may still be appropriate “as a first measure” in¿“extreme cases” where a litigant violates a court order and “persists in the outright refusal to comply with [its] discovery obligations.”  (Id.)  This is such a case.  

Plaintiff served four sets of discovery, and responses were due in May 2026, nearly four months ago.  Defendants did not respond by July 21, 2026, the deadline imposed in the Court’s July 1, 2026 order.  Monetary sanctions have also failed to motivate Defendants to respond, and indeed, Defendants have failed to even pay the sanctions.  Accordingly, the Court concludes that terminating sanctions are warranted.  The Court strikes Defendants’ answer and enters default against them. 

As to Plaintiff’s request for monetary sanctions, the Court concludes that its entry of default against Defendants is a sufficient remedy for Defendants’ failures to participate in the discovery process.¿ It is a waste of the Court’s time and resources to evaluate a sanctions request when Defendants have not paid prior sanctions, and they are subject to the ultimate sanction of termination.   

CONCLUSION 

 

Based on the foregoing, the Court GRANTS IN PART and DENIES IN PART Plaintiff’s motion for terminating sanctions.  The Court strikes Defendants’ answer, enters default against Defendants and sets a hearing on October 30, 2026 to consider Plaintiff’s request for entry of default judgment.  Plaintiff must file a default package within 10 days of the hearing.   

     

IT IS SO ORDERED. 

 

DATED: September 15, 2026 ___________________________ 

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court
